chapter_summary:
Creating comprehensive architectural documentation is a significant achievement, but its value is only realized if it is effectively communicated and continuously evolved. Documentation that sits unread in a dusty corner or quickly becomes outdated is essentially useless. The architect's role extends beyond design and initial documentation; it encompasses ensuring that the architectural knowledge is shared, understood, and remains relevant throughout the system's lifecycle. This involves strategic communication, proactive maintenance, and fostering a culture where documentation is seen as an integral part of the development process, not an afterthought.

Effective communication of architectural documentation requires tailoring the message to the audience. A detailed UML diagram might be perfect for a developer, but a business stakeholder needs a high-level overview focusing on business value and strategic alignment.
*   For **development teams**, detailed architectural views (logical, development, process) and ADRs are crucial. These can be communicated through dedicated workshops, walk-throughs, and by making them easily accessible in version control or internal wikis. Live coding sessions that demonstrate how the architecture translates into code can be highly effective.
*   For **operations teams**, the physical (deployment) view, along with operational runbooks and monitoring strategies, is paramount. Communication often involves joint sessions where deployment procedures, scaling strategies, and disaster recovery plans are reviewed.
*   For **business stakeholders and management**, high-level conceptual diagrams, architectural roadmaps, and summaries of key decisions (often derived from ADRs) are more appropriate. These should focus on how the architecture supports business goals, manages risk, and enables future growth. Presentations and executive summaries are common formats.

A critical challenge is keeping documentation current with an evolving codebase. Software systems are rarely static; new features are added, bugs are fixed, and refactoring occurs constantly. Outdated documentation can lead to confusion, incorrect assumptions, and ultimately, architectural erosion. To combat this, architects must embrace strategies for continuous documentation. One powerful approach is **"documentation as code."** This paradigm treats documentation artifacts (like ADRs, architectural diagrams, and system descriptions) as code.
*   **Version Control:** Store documentation in the same version control system (e.g., Git) as the source code. This ensures that documentation changes are tracked, reviewed, and linked to specific code changes.
*   **Plain Text/Markdown:** Write documentation in plain text formats like Markdown, AsciiDoc, or reStructuredText. These are easy to read, diff, and integrate into automated workflows.
*   **Automated Generation:** Use tools to generate diagrams (e.g., PlantUML, Mermaid.js, Structurizr) or documentation sites (e.g., MkDocs, Sphinx) directly from code or configuration files. This reduces manual effort and ensures consistency. For instance, a PlantUML diagram can be defined in a `.puml` file, versioned, and automatically rendered into an image as part of the CI/CD pipeline. If the underlying code structure changes, the diagram definition can be updated in the same pull request.

```plantuml
@startuml
actor "Client" as client
boundary "API Gateway" as api_gateway
control "User Service" as user_service
database "User DB" as user_db
control "Product Service" as product_service
database "Product DB" as product_db

client -> api_gateway : Request
api_gateway --> user_service : Authenticate
user_service --> user_db : Query User
user_service --> api_gateway : Auth Token
api_gateway --> product_service : Get Products
product_service --> product_db : Query Products
product_service --> api_gateway : Product Data
api_gateway --> client : Response
@enduml
```
This PlantUML snippet, when rendered, produces a sequence diagram. Storing this in Git and rendering it automatically means the diagram is always up-to-date with its definition.

Tools like **Arc42** (a lightweight documentation template) and **C4 Model** (a hierarchical approach to diagramming software architecture) also promote structured and maintainable documentation. The C4 Model, for example, encourages documenting at different levels of abstraction: Context, Containers, Components, and Code. This progressive detail helps manage complexity and ensures that documentation is relevant to different audiences.

The architect plays a pivotal role in fostering a documentation culture. This involves:
*   **Leading by Example:** Consistently documenting their own architectural decisions and designs.
*   **Providing Templates and Tools:** Making it easy for others to contribute to documentation (e.g., ADR templates, diagramming tools).
*   **Integrating into Workflow:** Making documentation a natural part of design, development, and code review processes. For instance, a pull request for a significant feature might require an updated architectural diagram or a new ADR.
*   **Training and Mentoring:** Educating the team on the importance and best practices of documentation.
*   **Regular Reviews:** Periodically reviewing documentation for accuracy and relevance, perhaps as part of architectural review boards.

By treating documentation as a first-class artifact, integrating it into automated workflows, and cultivating a supportive culture, organizations can ensure that their architectural knowledge remains alive, accurate, and valuable, driving better design decisions and enabling sustainable system evolution. The safety note here is to avoid the trap of "big upfront documentation" which quickly becomes obsolete. Instead, aim for "just enough" documentation that is continuously maintained and evolved alongside the code.

screens.title: Communicating and Evolving Architectural Documentation
screens.subtitle: Make architecture readable, maintainable, and part of everyday development

narration.text: Architectural documentation only delivers value when people read it, trust it, and act on it. In this lesson you will learn how to tailor documentation for different audiences, keep it aligned with an evolving codebase, and set up routines and tooling that make documentation part of development rather than an afterthought. We will explore documentation as code: putting ADRs, diagram definitions, and runbooks into version control, using plain text formats that diff well, and automating diagram rendering. You will see concrete practices like using PlantUML or Mermaid. js files, integrating renders into CI, and creating concise executive summaries for stakeholders. We will also discuss the architect’s role in leading by example, providing templates, and embedding documentation tasks into pull request workflows. By the end of this chapter you should be able to choose the right level of detail for an audience, set up basic automation so diagrams stay current, and foster small, repeatable habits that prevent architectural erosion. Think about one piece of architecture you work on now — how would you make its documentation easier to find and keep current?

keyIdea.text: Treat documentation as a first-class artifact: tailor it to audience needs, store it with code, and automate updates to keep it accurate as systems change.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to tailor architectural documentation to different audiences, set up basic documentation-as-code workflows, and keep documentation current with continuous practices. screens.title: Why communication and evolution matter
screens.subtitle: From static documents to living knowledge

narration.text: Architecture documentation is a design asset only when it is read, trusted, and updated. A static document that sits alone becomes stale and encourages incorrect assumptions, which can lead to architectural erosion where the actual system drifts from the documented design. To avoid that, treat documentation as living knowledge: it should be easy to find, quick to update, and linked to the changes it describes. A concrete example is a service that changes its A P I without a corresponding update to deployment diagrams and runbooks; operations teams may follow an outdated procedure during an incident. A common misconception is that more documentation equals better documentation. In truth, excessive upfront detail that is never maintained is worse than a few concise, well-maintained views. Aim for 'just enough' documentation: the minimal set of views and ADRs that enable understanding and decision-making. Practically, that means producing targeted artifacts for the intended audience and establishing a lightweight rhythm of updates and reviews. As a quick check, ask yourself: can a new team member perform a common task using only your current docs? If not, prioritize the pieces that enable that task.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Living documentation is accessible, concise, and updated regularly to reflect real system behavior and decisions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Why communication and evolution matter
Living documentation: a working definition
Documentation that is discoverable, accurate, and maintained as part of normal development activity.
Why it matters
Prevents mismatches between design and implementation, reduces incident handling time, and helps onboarding.
Common mistake
Equating volume with quality. Big, unmaintained docs cause more harm than a few maintained artifacts.
Key Takeaway

Focus on discoverability and maintenance cycles. Small, frequent updates beat large, stale documents.

Concrete scenario
A service changes how it authenticates users. Without an updated diagram or runbook, deployments and incidents use old steps and cause friction.
Actionable sample
Require an ADR and a small deployment note in the pull request when authentication logic or endpoints change.
Check your understanding
Does your team have a checklist item in pull requests to update relevant docs? If not, add one for a week and observe the effect.

screens.title: Tailoring documentation to your audience
screens.subtitle: What developers, ops, and executives need to know

narration.text: Different audiences need different artifacts and levels of detail. Developers typically need logical and development views, ADRs, and component-level diagrams. These artifacts show interfaces, data flows, and implementation notes that make coding and refactoring decisions straightforward. Operations teams rely on the physical or deployment view, runbooks, monitoring strategies, and scaling notes; they need concrete steps they can run in an incident. Executives and business stakeholders benefit from concise conceptual diagrams, roadmaps, and executive summaries focused on risk, cost, and business impact. A common misconception is to present the same diagram to all groups. That leads to either overwhelming non-technical stakeholders or omitting crucial details developers require. A concrete example is an A P I change: developers need updated component diagrams and code samples, ops need updated deployment and migration steps, and executives need a short note on customer impact and timeline. The practical takeaway is to maintain a small set of artifacts per audience, link them together, and keep summaries that translate technical changes into business terms. Tailoring documentation to your audience means produce targeted artifacts: detailed technical views for developers, runbooks for ops, and concise summaries for executives.. In practical terms, what developers, ops, and executives need to know. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audience strategy
keyIdea.text: Produce targeted artifacts: detailed technical views for developers, runbooks for ops, and concise summaries for executives.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Tailoring documentation to your audience
Three audience profiles
Developers
ADRs, component and code-level diagrams, and example code or test cases to validate design choices.
Operations
Deployment topology, runbooks, monitoring strategies, scaling and recovery steps.
Executives
High-level diagrams, roadmaps, and risk/benefit summaries that connect architecture to business goals.
Practical pattern
Keep a compact set of artifacts that map to roles. Link them: an ADR references a component diagram; the diagram links to a deployment view and to runbooks as needed.
Concrete example
When changing an API, update a component diagram and ADR for developers, a migration runbook for ops, and a one-paragraph impact note for stakeholders.
Misconception check
Avoid one-size-fits-all diagrams. Tailor level of abstraction and language to the audience to avoid confusion.
Try this

Create a one-paragraph executive summary for a recent change and link it to a technical ADR and diagram in the repo.

narration.text: Keeping documentation aligned with a changing codebase requires a repeatable, lightweight process. Think of documentation as part of the continuous delivery loop: make a small set of rules and automate where possible. A suggested flow is four steps: identify when a change affects architecture, update the minimal artifacts (ADRs, diagrams, runbooks), submit them in the same pull request as the code, and review them as part of the normal PR process. For example, if a developer changes a data model, they should update the relevant component diagram and add a short ADR or note explaining the rationale. A common pitfall is treating documentation as optional; instead, require a documentation check in the PR checklist so updates are visible and reviewed. Automation helps: placing diagrams in version control and rendering them in CI ensures a rendered image matches the text definition. Regular reviews, perhaps quarterly, catch drift and encourage corrections. The key is small, frequent updates tied to code changes rather than large, infrequent documentation pushes. Keeping documentation current means make documentation updates part of the pull-request lifecycle: change, document, pr, review, and automate renders to keep artifacts current.. In practical terms, a lightweight continuous documentation loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Continuous loop
keyIdea.text: Make documentation updates part of the pull-request lifecycle: change, document, PR, review, and automate renders to keep artifacts current.

Four-step continuous loop
1
Detect impact
Identify code changes that affect architecture or operations.
2
Update artifacts
Make minimal updates to ADRs, diagrams, and runbooks that are affected.
3
Include in PR
Place documentation changes in the same pull request as the code change.
4
Review and automate
Review docs as part of code review and use CI to render diagrams automatically.
Concrete example
A developer changes a REST contract. They update the component diagram file, add a short ADR describing the rationale, and include both in the feature PR. CI renders the updated diagram so reviewers can verify correctness visually.
Common pitfall
Relying on manual checks without automation. Manual steps are easy to forget during busy sprints.
Key Takeaway

Tie documentation updates to code changes and automate rendering to reduce drift and increase trust.

screens.title: Documentation as Code
screens.subtitle: Principles: version control, plain text, and automation

narration.text: Documentation as code treats documentation artifacts the same way we treat source code: they live in version control, are written in text formats, and are included in automated pipelines where possible. The key elements are version control for traceability and diffs, plain-text formats like Markdown or AsciiDoc for readability and easy diffs, and automated generation or rendering of diagrams and sites. A concrete example is storing a PlantUML definition file in the repository, updating it in the same pull request as related code, and letting CI render it into an image that is published to the internal documentation site. This approach enables reviewers to see the diffs for documentation changes, link changes to code commits, and roll back if needed. A common misconception is that text-based diagrams are inferior visually; in practice, text definitions improve maintainability and can be rendered with consistent styling automatically. The practical benefit is reduced maintenance cost and stronger linkage between decisions, code, and visualizations. Documentation as Code means treat docs like code: version them, write them in plain text, and automate rendering to keep visuals consistent and reviewable.. In practical terms, principles: version control, plain text, and automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Principle
keyIdea.text: Treat docs like code: version them, write them in plain text, and automate rendering to keep visuals consistent and reviewable.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Documentation as Code
Core elements
  • Version control: Track who changed what and when so documentation history is auditable.
  • Plain text: Use Markdown, AsciiDoc, or similar formats for readable diffs and easy editing.
  • Automation: Render diagrams and publish docs as part of CI to ensure visuals reflect definitions.
Misconception
Text-based diagrams are not lower quality; they enable automation and consistent styling which speeds maintenance.
Concrete workflow
Place ADRs and diagram definitions next to the code they describe. When the code changes, update the artifacts in the same pull request. Use CI to render diagrams and publish them to your docs portal.
Tool examples
PlantUML, Mermaid.js for text diagrams; MkDocs and Sphinx to build documentation sites from text files.
Key Takeaway

Using plain text and automation reduces friction and keeps documentation aligned with code changes.

screens.title: Example: PlantUML in the repository
screens.subtitle: A text-based diagram file rendered automatically

narration.text: Let's look at a typical PlantUML snippet used as a repository artifact and how it supports documentation as code. The snippet defines actors, boundaries, controls, and databases to describe request flows among services. When stored as a. puml file in Git, the text can be reviewed in a pull request and rendered in CI so reviewers see the updated picture without manual editing. For example, a sequence that shows a client hitting an A P I gateway, the gateway authenticating with a user service, and then requesting product data from a product service is directly captured in text. A common misconception is that diagrams must be drawn in a GUI tool. In contrast, defining the diagram in text makes changes diffable and easily reviewed. A practical check: when you update a service interaction, update the. puml file in the same pull request and confirm the CI job produces the new render. This links intent, decision, and visual evidence in a single change set. Example: PlantUML in the repository means store plantuml definitions in the repo, update them with related code changes, and render them in ci for reliable visuals and reviewability.. In practical terms, a text-based diagram file rendered automatically. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Store PlantUML definitions in the repo, update them with related code changes, and render them in CI for reliable visuals and reviewability.

PlantUML snippet (store as .puml)
@startuml actor "Client" as client boundary "API Gateway" as api_gateway control "User Service" as user_service database "User DB" as user_db control "Product Service" as product_service database "Product DB" as product_db client -> api_gateway : Request api_gateway --> user_service : Authenticate user_service --> user_db : Query User user_service --> api_gateway : Auth Token api_gateway --> product_service : Get Products product_service --> product_db : Query Products product_service --> api_gateway : Product Data api_gateway --> client : Response @enduml
Place this file next to the code that defines service interfaces. When a related change is submitted, update the .puml in the same pull request so reviewers see both code and diagram diffs.
Practical notes
  • CI can run PlantUML to render images automatically and publish them to the docs portal.
  • Diffs of .puml files are readable and make review straightforward.
  • Keep naming conventions and directories consistent so artifacts are easy to find.
Key Takeaway

Text-based diagram definitions let you version, diff, and automate visuals alongside code changes.

narration.text: Structured templates help manage complexity by providing consistent levels of abstraction. The C4 Model divides documentation into Context, Container, Component, and Code, which helps you present the right amount of detail to each audience. Arc42 is a lightweight template that provides sections for decisions, constraints, and views. Using these models reduces guesswork about what to document and where to place it. A concrete example: when introducing a new microservice, use a C4 Context diagram to show its relationship with other systems for stakeholders, a Container diagram to show deployment and runtime concerns for operations, and a Component diagram to help developers see internal structure. A common misconception is that templates are bureaucratic; in practice, they speed contribution by reducing uncertainty. The practical step is to adopt one model across the organization, provide a starter template in the repo, and require minimal completed sections when an ADR or component is created. C4 Model and Arc42 means use the c4 model or arc42 to provide consistent views and make it easier for contributors to know what to document.. In practical terms, structured templates for multi-level documentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Structured templates
keyIdea.text: Use the C4 Model or Arc42 to provide consistent views and make it easier for contributors to know what to document.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › C4 Model and Arc42
C4 Model levels
  • Context: high-level relationships and stakeholders.
  • Container: runtime and deployment concerns.
  • Component: internal structure and responsibilities.
  • Code: low-level implementation details.
Arc42
A template-based approach covering decisions, constraints, and views to create consistent documentation artifacts.
Concrete workflow
Keep a repository folder with a template README for each service that contains C4 context and container skeletons, plus ADR placeholders. Encourage contributors to complete the minimal fields when making changes.
Misconception check
Templates are not paperwork. They reduce friction by making the expected content explicit and easy to fill.
Key Takeaway

Adopt one structured approach and provide starter templates to make documentation a quick, repeatable task.

screens.title: Activity: Document a microservice interaction
screens.subtitle: Practice PlantUML and ADRs for a payment-order flow

narration.text: This hands-on activity asks you to document a microservice interaction using a text-based diagram and an ADR. The scenario: a user places an order, the order service calls the payment service, and the order status is updated based on payment success or failure. Your goals are to write a PlantUML sequence that captures the messages, include an alt block for success and failure, and create a short ADR describing the decision for synchronous or asynchronous payment processing. Practically, create a. puml file with actors for the User and a boundary for the Web App, control components for Order Service and Payment Service, and databases for Order DB and Payment DB. Add messages for placing the order, initiating payment, and handling success or failure. In the ADR, record alternatives considered, the chosen approach, and consequences. A common pitfall is overcomplicating the diagram; keep messages focused on the interaction you want to teach. After completing the files, place them in a branch, open a pull request, and let CI render the diagram so reviewers can see both text diffs and the rendered image.

keyIdea.title: Practice
keyIdea.text: Create a PlantUML sequence and a short ADR. Place both in a PR so the rendered diagram and the rationale are reviewed together.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Activity: Document a microservice interaction
Task checklist
Write a PlantUML sequence
Include User actor, Web App boundary, Order and Payment services, and databases. Use an alt block for success and failure.
Create an ADR
Capture the decision about payment flow, alternatives, and consequences in a short ADR file.
Open a PR
Place the .puml and ADR in the same pull request and let CI render the diagram so reviewers can verify both code and visuals.
Hints and pitfalls
  • Keep the diagram focused on the interaction; avoid showing unrelated subsystems.
  • In the ADR, limit text to context, decision, reasoning, and consequences — keep it concise.
  • Use CI to render so reviewers see the visual and the textual diff together.
Key Takeaway

A short, versioned diagram plus an ADR in the same PR provides both visual and rationale context for reviewers.

narration.text: Automated generation and manual diagramming each have a place. Manual drawing tools can be quick for one-off visuals or whiteboard captures, but they often produce binary files that don't diff well and are hard to maintain. Automated approaches like PlantUML or Mermaid. js use text definitions that are versionable and can be rendered consistently in CI. The primary benefit of automation is maintainability: diffs reveal what changed, and renders can be regenerated as part of a pipeline. A common misconception is to assume automation eliminates human review. It does not; reviewers still check the meaning and accuracy of diagrams. Use automation when diagrams represent system structure or flows that evolve with code, and use manual tools sparingly for brainstorming or presentation-ready visuals that will be converted into maintainable artifacts later. A practical pattern is to author a text diagram from the start and convert hand-drawn sketches into a text definition as part of follow-up work so the artifact becomes maintainable. Automated generation vs manual diagrams means prefer text-defined diagrams for maintainability; use manual tools for quick sketches but convert to versioned text when the artifact is worth keeping.. In practical terms, trade-offs and best uses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Prefer text-defined diagrams for maintainability; use manual tools for quick sketches but convert to versioned text when the artifact is worth keeping.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Automated generation vs manual diagrams
Manual diagrams
Good for quick communication and brainstorming but usually produce binary artifacts that are hard to diff and maintain.
When to use
Sketching, whiteboard captures, early brainstorming. Convert to versioned text if the artifact will be kept.
Automated generation
Text-based definitions that render into consistent visuals, suitable for diagrams that evolve with code.
When to use
Architecture views, sequence flows, and diagrams tied to ongoing development. They support diffs, reviews, and CI rendering.
Key Takeaway

Prefer text-defined diagrams for maintainability; only keep manual images for transient or presentation tasks unless converted later.

screens.title: Fostering a documentation culture
screens.subtitle: Roles, templates, training, and regular reviews

narration.text: Culture changes require consistent leadership and low-friction processes. Architects can foster a documentation culture by leading with examples: publish ADRs, keep diagram definitions next to code, and use templates that reduce cognitive overhead for contributors. Provide training and short onboarding sessions that show how to write ADRs, create a diagram file, and include both in pull requests. Integrate documentation checks into reviews and set a clear rule for when a change requires an ADR or update. Regular review cadences, such as quarterly or tied to milestone delivery, help find drift and correct inconsistencies. A common pitfall is imposing heavy governance; instead, prefer lightweight rules that are enforced by habit and tooling. For instance, a small PR checklist item and a CI job that fails when diagram renders are missing can be effective without being punitive. The goal is to make documentation the path of least resistance rather than an afterthought. Fostering a documentation culture means lead by example, provide templates and training, and embed lightweight review steps so documentation becomes a natural part of delivery.. In practical terms, roles, templates, training, and regular reviews. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Culture
keyIdea.text: Lead by example, provide templates and training, and embed lightweight review steps so documentation becomes a natural part of delivery.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Fostering a documentation culture
Practical roles
  • Lead by example: architects publish ADRs and update diagrams themselves.
  • Provide templates: ADR skeletons, diagram folders, PR checklists.
  • Train: short demos and mentoring to lower the barrier to contribute.
Lightweight enforcement
Use small rules that are easy to follow: PR checklist items, CI rendering, and occasional documentation review meetings. Avoid heavy processes that discourage contributors.
Key Takeaway

Make it easy and expected to document; tool support and small habits win over heavy governance.

narration.text: A minimal checklist helps teams adopt consistent behavior. Start with a short list: one, place ADRs and diagram definitions in the repository with the code they describe; two, use plain-text formats for diffability; three, include documentation changes in the same pull request as code changes; four, render diagrams automatically and publish them; and five, hold periodic reviews to detect drift. Each item reduces the chance of stale documentation. For a concrete example, require that any change to service interfaces also adds or updates a component diagram file and a one-paragraph ADR summary in the PR. A common misconception is that checklists slow development. In reality, short, well-chosen checklist items prevent larger rewrites and debugging time later. Implement these checklist items as part of your PR template and pair them with CI jobs that surface missing renders or broken links so contributors get immediate feedback. narration.text: Remember these core concepts as you improve your architectural documentation. First, tailor artifacts to the audience: provide technical diagrams for developers, deployment views and runbooks for operations, and concise summaries for business stakeholders.
